reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: Presents with persistent polyuria and polydipsia, typically with large volumes of dilute (hypotonic) urine and a strong thirst that drives high fluid intake
The key distinction is between central DI, from deficient vasopressin secretion, and nephrogenic DI, from renal resistance to vasopressin
Primary polydipsia, in which excessive drinking suppresses vasopressin, must be separated from true DI as management differs completely
Serum sodium is often high-normal or elevated in true DI, whereas primary polydipsia tends toward low-normal sodium
A water deprivation test with subsequent desmopressin assesses urinary concentrating ability and response to exogenous hormone
Copeptin measurement, particularly after hypertonic saline stimulation, is increasingly used as a more reliable discriminator
Central DI usually responds to desmopressin, whereas nephrogenic DI is managed by treating the underlying cause and supportive measures
Where thirst perception is intact and access to water is preserved, patients can defend their sodium; the danger is when thirst or water access is impaired
reference.pathophysiology: Diabetes insipidus reflects an inability to concentrate urine appropriately. In central (cranial) DI there is deficient secretion of arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) due to disease of the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary, such as tumours, infiltrative disease, trauma, or surgery. In nephrogenic DI the kidney fails to respond to circulating vasopressin, from inherited receptor or aquaporin defects, drugs such as lithium, hypercalcaemia, or hypokalaemia. In both, the collecting duct cannot reabsorb enough free water, producing large volumes of dilute urine; if water intake cannot keep pace, plasma osmolality and sodium rise. Primary polydipsia is a separate entity in which excessive fluid intake physiologically suppresses vasopressin.
additionalDifferentials: Osmotic diuresis from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (hyperglycaemia)
Hypercalcaemia or hypokalaemia causing acquired nephrogenic DI
Chronic kidney disease with impaired concentrating ability
additionalInvestigations: Paired serum and urine osmolality with serum sodium
24-hour urine volume to confirm true polyuria
Water deprivation test followed by desmopressin challenge
Plasma copeptin, ideally with hypertonic saline or arginine stimulation
Serum glucose, calcium, and potassium to exclude secondary causes
Pituitary and hypothalamic MRI when central DI is confirmed to seek a structural or infiltrative lesion
redFlags: Rapidly rising sodium with altered consciousness from unreplaced free water losses
DI arising after pituitary surgery or head injury, which may fluctuate through a triphasic pattern
Absent or impaired thirst (adipsic DI) predisposing to dangerous hypernatraemia
Loss of a previously present suprasellar lesion signal or new mass suggesting infiltrative or neoplastic disease
reference.prognosis: Central DI is generally well controlled with vasopressin replacement and normal life expectancy when thirst and water access are intact; nephrogenic DI depends on reversibility of the underlying cause, and adipsic forms carry ongoing risk of severe sodium disturbances.
pitfalls: Confusing osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia with true DI
Giving desmopressin to a patient with primary polydipsia and precipitating water intoxication
Restricting fluids in a patient who cannot concentrate urine, causing hypernatraemic dehydration
Overlooking lithium or hypercalcaemia as reversible causes of nephrogenic DI
management: Central diabetes insipidus: replace vasopressin with desmopressin, titrated to control polyuria while avoiding dilutional hyponatraemia
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: remove reversible causes such as lithium, correct hypercalcaemia and hypokalaemia, and use thiazide diuretics, amiloride and a low-sodium, low-protein diet
Ensure free access to water and match intake to output with careful fluid-balance monitoring
Treat any underlying hypothalamic or pituitary lesion driving central disease
Monitor serum sodium, plasma and urine osmolality and urine output to detect over- or under-treatment
Structured fluid prescription with heightened caution in adipsic forms to prevent severe sodium disturbance
Refer to endocrinology, escalating acutely for hypernatraemia or dehydration during intercurrent illness
